clue.text: Straightforward bill, similar to white paper

parts.note: a bill is a narrow headland, as in Portland Bill, also called a point
unmarked white paper is blank

explanation.surface: A bill in Parliament is as plain and simple as a white paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bill' and 'white paper' look like parliamentary documents; here bill is a headland. Portland Bill is a promontory on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A point-blank remark is blunt and direct, with nothing held back.

clue.text: City given little opening in goalless draw

indicators.note: puts the opening word between the two letters of the draw

parts.note: a goalless draw is nil-nil, two zeros written as two Os
a port is a small opening in a ship's side

explanation.surface: A football match ends nil-nil in a city, with few chances.
explanation.definitionFit: Oporto is a city in northern Portugal, home of port wine.

clue.text: Songbird making madman brood

parts.note: a nut is slang for a crazy person
a hatch is a brood of young birds

explanation.surface: A bird drives a madman to brood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brood' looks like a verb for worrying; it is a noun, a clutch of chicks.
explanation.definitionFit: The nuthatch is a small climbing songbird that wedges nuts in bark to crack them.

clue.text: Get into jet, initially, that's used for instruction

indicators.note: puts the jet word first in the answer

parts.note: jet black is a deep black
to board a ship or plane is to get into it

explanation.surface: Getting on a jet is the first step in a flying lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jet' looks like an aircraft to get into; it is the black stone.
explanation.definitionFit: A blackboard is a dark surface teachers write on with chalk.

clue.text: Germ-free, as it is up in space, possibly

indicators.note: puts the turned word inside the rearranged letters
possibly signals the letters of the word space could be arranged another way
in a down clue, up means the word it is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Is it germ-free up in outer space?
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' and 'is' are links; 'space' looks like outer space, but 'possibly' makes it anagram fodder (ASEPC), and 'up' turns the word it before it goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Aseptic means free from bacteria and infection, sterile.

clue.text: Human body as material, say, for painter

indicators.note: say signals a word spoken that is spelt differently

parts.note: clay is the human body seen as mere earthy matter

explanation.surface: An artist uses the human body as his medium.
explanation.walkthrough: Clay, the flesh as mortal matter, as in feet of clay, sounds like the name of the artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Klee was a Swiss-German painter of colourful abstract works.

clue.text: Not certain how to describe pudding before it's eaten?

definitions.text: how to describe pudding before it's eaten?

explanation.surface: Wondering about a dessert before tasting it.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'the proof of the pudding is in the eating' means a pudding is untested until eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unproven is unsure; by the proverb, a pudding has had no test until someone eats it.

clue.text: Thus, king's surrounded by too serious types

parts.note: so means thus

indicators.note: puts the king letter inside the word for too

parts.note: besides means also, too
R, for rex, is the abbreviation for king; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: So the king is hemmed in by overly earnest courtiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'too serious' reads as one phrase, but 'too' is the wordplay and 'serious types' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sobersides are solemn, humourless people.

clue.text: Having no surplus weight to shed

parts.note: lean means carrying no fat
taken as written

explanation.surface: A slimmer has no excess weight left to lose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shed' looks like a verb meaning lose, as in shedding pounds, but it is the noun: a simple outbuilding.
explanation.definitionFit: A lean-to is a small shed built against a wall, its roof sloping off the main building.

clue.text: A certain distance, people must go in this

definitions.text: A certain distance, people must go in this

parts.note: a foot is a fixed measure of length
a race is a people, a group sharing descent

explanation.surface: Everyone has to cover a set distance in this event.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines a running contest on foot while also giving the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A footrace is a running contest over a set course that competitors must complete on foot.

clue.text: Protect page in front of book

indicators.note: places the page letter before the next piece in the answer

parts.note: to book a table is to reserve it

explanation.surface: A notice tells you to keep safe the page before the front of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: To preserve something is to keep it safe from harm or decay.

clue.text: Gunman's horse

explanation.surface: The cowboy's horse, as in any Western.
explanation.definitionFit: A Colt is a revolver, a gunman's weapon, and a young male horse is a colt.

clue.text: Pictures of girls making a tart

explanation.surface: Glamour photographs of girls making a pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheesecake is slang for pin-up photos of women, and also a rich dessert on a pastry or biscuit base.

clue.text: Synopsis survives for Aubrey's book

parts.note: a brief is a short summary of a case
lives means stays alive

explanation.surface: A summary outlasts the work written by Aubrey.
explanation.walkthrough: John Aubrey was a 17th-century English antiquary whose gossipy biographical sketches carry this title.
explanation.definitionFit: Brief Lives is the title of John Aubrey's collection of short biographies.

clue.text: Theatre's opening, initially, near West End

parts.note: initially means first
nigh is an old word for near

indicators.note: end picks the final letter of the word west

explanation.surface: A theatre opens its doors near London's West End.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West End' looks like London's theatre district, which fits the surface; 'End' takes the last letter of West.
explanation.definitionFit: A first night is the opening performance of a play.

clue.text: Possible choice of better approach by a head

indicators.note: means beside, so one piece sits next to the other

parts.note: each means per head, as in five pounds each
a way is an approach or method

explanation.surface: A punter considers a horse that might win by a head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better' is one who bets, not 'superior'. An each-way bet backs a horse both to win and to be placed.
explanation.definitionFit: Betting each way is an option for a punter, covering a win and a place.

clue.text: Old woman embracing best friend of a Girl Guide

indicators.note: puts the friend word inside the old woman word

parts.note: a crone is an old woman
diamonds are a girl's best friend, and ice is slang for diamonds

explanation.surface: An old woman hugs the best friend of a Girl Guide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Girl Guide' looks like the youth movement; 'Guide' is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A cicerone is a guide who shows sightseers around places of interest.

clue.text: Went on track and prepared for race

explanation.surface: An athlete practised on the track before the big event.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelling by rail on a track is going by train; an athlete who has practised for a race is in condition.

clue.text: Triumph or disaster for a cheat. (If you remember)

explanation.surface: Success and failure both deceive us, as a poem reminds.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's poem If says to meet Triumph and Disaster and treat those two impostors just the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling calls triumph and disaster deceivers; a cheat is one who poses falsely as someone else.

clue.text: Apprentice getting a pound in pay?

parts.note: L, from libra, is the symbol for a pound
someone in paid work is an earner

explanation.surface: A trainee gets a single pound in wages.
explanation.definitionFit: A learner is a trainee still acquiring a trade.

clue.text: Defeat after short time? Come off it!

indicators.note: puts the defeat word after the time word in the answer

parts.note: a second is a brief moment
to best someone is to beat them

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at a claim of winning in record time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come off it!' looks like a scoff, but 'it' stands for the answer: to come off second best is to lose.
explanation.definitionFit: In the idiom 'come off second best', the phrase names the loser's place, so 'come off it' completes it.

clue.text: Go through difficult situation while away

explanation.surface: Travellers get through a tricky spot while abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass is to go through; things come to a pretty pass when difficult; to pass time is to spend it idly.

clue.text: Sudden blow makes one cry out

explanation.surface: A sudden blow makes someone yell.
explanation.definitionFit: A squall is a sudden gust of wind, and to squall is to scream noisily like a baby.

clue.text: Drinker gets to wake in vehicle

indicators.note: puts the waking word inside the vehicle word

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
to rouse is to wake someone

explanation.surface: A drunk is woken up in a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A carouser drinks heavily in noisy revelry.

clue.text: Turn made a big impression

explanation.surface: A turn on stage was a great success.
explanation.definitionFit: To slew is to swing round; slew, past of slay, is slang for wowing an audience.

clue.text: Patching tattered old headgear

indicators.note: tattered means torn to pieces, so the letters of the word before are rearranged

explanation.surface: Mending a worn-out old hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightcap was a cloth cap worn in bed in former times.

clue.text: Brand left with point in fire

parts.note: a brand or make is a kind
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A burning stick is pushed into the fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brand' looks like a burning torch to go with fire; it means type or make.
explanation.definitionFit: To kindle is to set alight, to fire.

clue.text: Labour to control industrial action

parts.note: labour is work
taken as written
to rule is to control

explanation.surface: The Labour Party moves to control strikes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the British political party; here it just means toil.
explanation.definitionFit: A work-to-rule is a protest in which employees follow regulations so strictly that output slows.
